_note: Measures that are not daily indicators in the app: what they are, how often, and why. Only facts from the cited sources; frequency is ours where the source gives none (marked 'our plan').

items.how: Mass measurement device: it pushes the astronaut with a known force and computes mass from the acceleration (there is no weight in orbit).
items.why: Losing mass shows not enough food or muscle loss.

items.how: Bone scan (DXA) before and after the mission; calcium in urine as a sign of bone breaking down.
items.how_often: scan before and after flight; urine samples during flight
items.why: Astronauts can lose up to 1-2% of bone density per month in the hip and spine, compared with 0.5-1% per year in older people on Earth. Bone breaking down also raises calcium in urine, a kidney stone risk.

items.how: Samples collected and analysed for biochemical markers.
items.why: Shows changes in nutrition, bones, kidneys and metabolism that daily numbers miss.

items.how: Blood and saliva samples: stress hormones, viral reactivation, blood counts and cell types.
items.how_often: several times per mission, including the start of the flight
items.why: Launch and the first days are stressful; stress can wake up dormant viruses and weaken immunity.

items.how: 10 short computer tests (memory, attention, risk taking, emotion recognition and more), about 16 minutes on the station.
items.why: Catches slower thinking or riskier decisions before they cause mistakes.

items.how: A wrist monitor records movement and light exposure.
items.why: Shows real sleep and body-clock timing.

items.what: Balance, movement, heart rate and blood pressure tests
items.why: Gravity changes affect balance and blood pressure when standing up after landing.
